title: DeCovarT reproducibility
text:
0.1 How to render
This Quarto book is the narrative companion to the analysis scripts under scripts/. R chunks stay eval: false until artefacts exist. Mermaid and static Markdown still execute; freeze: auto caches those results in docs/_freeze.
The layout follows analysis reproducibility repos such as cellrank2_reproducibility (Python + Jupyter Book there). Here the stack is R, renv, and Quarto, published with the GitHub Pages gh-pages workflow (Quarto: GitHub Pages, Knitr with renv).
The scientific target is DeCovarT’s cell-type Gaussians: sparse precisions \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\equiv\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{-1}\) and means \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}\) estimated from labelled single-cell transcriptomes, then plugged into the bulk convolution. Notation follows the article Methods. Computation stays in scripts/; this book is theory, criticism, and design.
From the repository root, after renv::restore():
The book format is HTML only for now (pdf is commented in docs/_quarto.yml). CI publishes HTML to the gh-pages branch.

title: 3  Feature selection for cell-type Gaussians
text:
4 Notation
This chapter selects a gene panel \(\mathcal{G}\) on which DeCovarT can discriminate gastruloid cell types through both mean shifts \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}\) and precision rewiring \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\equiv\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{-1}\). Notation follows the article: gene \(g=1,\ldots,G\); cell type \(j=1,\ldots,J\); bulk \(\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}\) is a Gaussian convolution of purified profiles (Wang et al. 2019). Feature selection is a pre-modelling filter (Guyon and Elisseeff 2003), not a marker-enrichment score.
The first pipeline treated sctransform highly variable genes (HVGs), optional DESeq2 on technical pseudo-bulks, and an NSGA-II Pareto refinement as a single stack. That mix is too optimistic on Suppinger, where there is only one scRNA-seq resource (GEO GSE229513; (Suppinger et al. 2023)), and it puts variance stabilisation on the same design axis as the graphical model (see Chapter 6 and Note 6.1). Here we split the problem into a naive screen (cheap, marginally motivated) and an all-versus-all refinement (geometry of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}\) and rewiring of \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\)). INDEED and D-trace enter only as a perspective (Chapter 7).
Let \(\boldsymbol{\mu}=(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j})_{j=1}^{J}\in\mathbb{R}^{G\times J}\) be the mean signature and \(\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{J}\) the cell-type covariances. Conditionally on proportions \(\boldsymbol{p}\in\Delta^{J-1}\),
\[
\boldsymbol{y}\mid(\boldsymbol{\zeta},\boldsymbol{p})
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}\!\left(
\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},\,
\sum_{j=1}^{J}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
\right),
\quad
\boldsymbol{\zeta}=(\boldsymbol{\mu},\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\}),
\tag{4.1}\]
which is the DeCovarT convolution (article Methods; the same \(p_{j}^{2}\) scaling appears in the first pipeline’s aggregation algebra, corrected in Chapter 8). For a subset \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,G\}\) write \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}\) for the corresponding rows. The 2-norm condition number is
\[
\kappa_{2}(\boldsymbol{X})
=
\frac{\sigma_{\max}(\boldsymbol{X})}{\sigma_{\min}(\boldsymbol{X})}.
\tag{4.2}\]
Large \(\kappa_{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}})\) is multicollinearity of the mean design (Gong and Szustakowski 2013; Newman et al. 2015). It does not see precision rewiring. For a gastruloid continuum, neighbouring states are close in mean by construction; aggressive \(\kappa\)-minimisation then keeps a few lineage representatives and drops genes whose signal lives in \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\) (Wang et al. 2019).

title: 3  Feature selection for cell-type Gaussians
text:
5.1 Highly variable genes
Single-cell UMI tables mix depth noise with biological heterogeneity. Regularised negative-binomial regression in sctransform (Hafemeister et al. 2025) / Seurat::SCTransform separates the two via Pearson residuals (Hafemeister and Satija 2019)
\[
r_{cg}
=
\frac{y_{cg}-\hat{\mu}_{cg}}
{\sqrt{\hat{\mu}_{cg}+\hat{\mu}_{cg}^{2}/\hat{\theta}_{g}}},
\tag{5.1}\]
with library size as an offset and empirical-Bayes shrinkage of dispersions \(\hat{\theta}_{g}\). Residual variance is a ranking score for HVGs, not a Gaussian observation model for graphical lasso.
Practical rules for Suppinger:

Do not regress out cell type when ranking HVGs: that removes the inter-type signal the panel is meant to keep.
A design \(\sim\texttt{CellType}\) without intercept contrasts each labelled type against the global mean across types, which is closer to an all-versus-all HVG ranking than a global intercept.
Keep on the order of \(2{,}000\) residual-variable genes as \(\mathcal{G}_{0}\) before any GGM; estimating \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\) on the full transcriptome is unstable when \(G\gg n_{j}\) even with glasso (Friedman et al. 2008).
SCTransform is tied to HVG ranking, not a factorial “normalisation arm” of the GRN design (Chapter 6).







Note 5.1: :information_source: HVGs are not a GGM input



Pearson residuals are closer to homoscedastic than raw UMI counts, which is why they are popular before PCA. They are still a nonlinear residualisation. Feeding them indiscriminately into SILGGM silently changes the estimand of \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\) away from the latent Gaussian that DeCovarT wants at the population level. If a Gaussian GGM is used, prefer a copula / nonparanormal map on the same gene set (Section 7.1), or better a Poisson-lognormal latent Gaussian (Section 7.2).

title: 3  Feature selection for cell-type Gaussians
text:
5.2 Marker genes
Classical signatures score gene \(g\) for type \(j\) against the remaining types, then concatenate lists (Newman et al. 2015). Two specificity scores on the simplex of relative means
\[
\pi_{gj}
=
\frac{\mu_{gj}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{J}\mu_{g\ell}},
\qquad
\sum_{j}\pi_{gj}=1,
\tag{5.2}\]
are useful compaction tools, not all-versus-all selectors.
Shannon entropy \(H(g)=-\sum_{j}\pi_{gj}\log\pi_{gj}\) is small when mass concentrates on few types. Gini of the same shares is large when one type dominates. High Gini / low entropy flags one-versus-rest markers. They do not guarantee that the corresponding rows of \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) are linearly independent: two markers that separate different types can still be collinear as rows if those types co-express a shared programme. Concatenating the top-\(k\) genes per type therefore often inflates \(|\mathcal{G}|\) without improving \(\kappa_{2}\) (see Note 5.3).
Known gastruloid lineage markers (from the Suppinger atlas and companion literature) belong in \(\mathcal{G}_{0}\) as seeds, not as the whole panel. They are the natural starting points for Markov-boundary expansion once a GGM exists (Chapter 7).

title: 3  Feature selection for cell-type Gaussians
section: 5.3 Differential expression — only with biological replication
text:
5.3 Differential expression — only with biological replication
DESeq2, edgeR and limma–voom remain the workhorses of one-versus-rest ranking (Love et al. 2014). CIBERSORT-style pipelines keep genes with a loose adjusted \(p\) ordered by fold-change, then prune by \(\kappa\) (Newman et al. 2015). That logic does not transfer to Suppinger as a DE experiment.






Warning 5.2: :warning: Technical pseudo-bulks are not biological replicates



Cells from a common experimental unit are not independent biological replicates. Splitting or bootstrapping cells characterises technical / sampling variability; it does not manufacture between-organoid uncertainty. Treating cells, or random partitions of cells, as DESeq2 replicates inflates apparent degrees of freedom and produces false discoveries (Squair et al. 2021; Crowell et al. 2020). The improved pipeline is explicit: Suppinger is one technical scRNA-seq resource.
Use DESeq2 in this book only if independent biological replicates exist (distinct organoids / donors / experiments with the same labelled types). For GSE229513, skip calibrated DE \(p\)-values. Rank genes by residual variance, Gini / entropy, or a nested-model \(F\) statistic treated as a score, not as a \(p\)-value.


If a later gastruloid cohort with genuine replication becomes available (GSE250136 is a different stem-embryo resource, useful as external validation, not as extra Suppinger replicates), then donor-level pseudo-bulks are the correct DE unit (Crowell et al. 2020; Squair et al. 2021). Until then, the naive screen is HVG + markers, not HVG + DESeq2.






Warning 5.3: :warning: Limitation of one-versus-rest concatenation



The union of per-type markers is usually a multicollinear \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}\) that is still too large for stable NNLS / GLS / DeCovarT Fisher information (Newman et al. 2015). A global all-versus-all stage is required (Chapter 6).

title: 3  Feature selection for cell-type Gaussians
text:
6.1 Why mean-only \(\kappa\) is not enough
\(\kappa_{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}})\) diagnoses mean collinearity. In a gastruloid continuum it is intrinsically large. Two closely related types can share nearly collinear means and still differ in \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\). Mean-only pruning then under-represents adjacent or low-abundance states — exactly the types whose rewiring DeCovarT is meant to exploit. Use \(\kappa\) as a diagnostic, not as the sole selector.
A variance-weighted variant standardises rows by gene-wise uncertainties \(\tau_{g}^{2}\) and evaluates conditioning in the \((J-1)\)-dimensional contrast space induced by \(\sum_{j}p_{j}=1\) (package vignette supp-S6-feature-selection.qmd). Unweighted \(\kappa\) can favour quiet but biased genes (Gong and Szustakowski 2013).

title: 3  Feature selection for cell-type Gaussians
text:
6.2 Genetic algorithms
AutoGeneS searches subsets with a multi-objective genetic algorithm that minimises inter-population correlation while maximising centroid distance (Aliee and Theis 2021). The loss is already all-versus-all. Related multi-objective genetic searches appear in network module discovery; they are not DeCovarT-specific.
For this repository the planned optimiser is NSGA-II via mco::nsga2() (Mersmann et al. 2020), as in the package vignette. Encode genes as a mask in \([0,1]^{|\mathcal{G}_{0}|}\) (thresholded to a target size) or as a lower-dimensional embedding of gene blocks. Minimise at least

\(\kappa_{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}})\) (mean geometry);
average pairwise overlap \(\overline{\omega}\) of the \(J\) Gaussians \(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})\) (Melnykov et al. 2012, 2021).

MixSim defines pairwise overlap as the sum of the two misclassification probabilities under a Bayes / MAP rule, not as \(1\) minus a distance. That is a sharper estimand than “one minus Hellinger”. Optional analytic surrogates — Jeffreys (symmetric KL), Chernoff / Bhattacharyya, and the Bures–Wasserstein metric on \((\boldsymbol{\mu}_{j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})\) — belong on the same Pareto front (package vignette). They use both means and covariances, which AutoGeneS correlation / centroid objectives do not.






Note 6.1: :information_source: A DeCovarT-specific third objective (proposal)



The improved pipeline proposed adding Fisher identifiability of \(\boldsymbol{p}\) under Equation 4.1: maximise the smallest eigenvalue of the mixture information \(I_{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{p})\), or minimise its condition number. That objective is not in the literature corpus; it is a composition. It is the right scientific target — DeCovarT’s score depends on \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}\) and \(\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\) jointly — but it is proportion-dependent and more expensive than MixSim overlap. Keep it as a sensitivity objective on a shortlist of non-dominated panels, not as the only fitness. Do not collapse the front to a single “knee” without nested, leakage-free validation.


Keep several non-dominated panels. Report the whole front. Nested cross-validation, when biological replicates exist, must build HVGs, DEGs and the Pareto panel inside each outer fold; otherwise the panel leaks (Squair et al. 2021). With one Suppinger resource, the honest statement is: the panel is fitted on this atlas and must be challenged on an external gastruloid cohort.

title: 3  Feature selection for cell-type Gaussians
text:
6.3 Differential networks as candidate generators
DeCovarT benefits specifically from rewiring between populations. A gene that changes neighbourhood in \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\) is a better candidate than a gene that is merely highly variable. Two strategies exist.
Fit every \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\), then compare supports. Independent glasso / SILGGM fits (Section 7.1) yield per-type edges; the symmetric difference of supports, or the difference of partial correlations, ranks genes by differential connectivity. This is simple and matches the objects DeCovarT eventually needs, but each glasso is shrunk and the difference of two biased estimators is not a debiased estimator of \(\Delta_{j\ell}=\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}-\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\ell}\).
Estimate \(\Delta_{j\ell}\) directly. D-trace methods target the difference of precisions without necessarily reconstructing both graphs first (see Chapter 7). They cannot replace \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\) in the generative model — DeCovarT still needs each covariance individually — but they are attractive feature objectives when individual networks are fairly dense and the difference is sparse.
Either way, treat differential-network hits as candidates for the all-versus-all stage, not as the final panel. Concatenating one-versus-rest network genes repeats Note 5.3.

title: 3  Feature selection for cell-type Gaussians
section: 7.1 INDEED: an ad-hoc fusion of DE and differential partial correlation
text:
7.1 INDEED: an ad-hoc fusion of DE and differential partial correlation
INDEED fits a sparse precision per group, converts to partial correlations
\[
\mathrm{pc}_{gg'}^{(j)}
=
-\frac{\theta_{gg'}^{(j)}}
{\sqrt{\theta_{gg}^{(j)}\,\theta_{g'g'}^{(j)}}},
\qquad
\Delta\mathrm{pc}_{gg'}
=
\mathrm{pc}_{gg'}^{(j)}-\mathrm{pc}_{gg'}^{(\ell)},
\tag{7.1}\]
filters \(\Delta\mathrm{pc}\) with a permutation (or bootstrap) null, and forms an activity score that multiplies mean evidence by differential connectivity (Zuo et al. 2016)
\[
\mathrm{AS}_{g}
=
\bigl(-\log p_{g}^{\mathrm{DE}}\bigr)
\sum_{g'\neq g}
\bigl\lvert\Delta\mathrm{pc}_{gg'}\bigr\rvert
\,
\mathbf{1}\{\Delta\mathrm{pc}_{gg'}\ \text{significant}\}.
\tag{7.2}\]
Relative to pure DGE, this favours genes whose undirected neighbourhood (Markov boundary in the GGM) differs between groups. Related ideas appear in weighted glasso pipelines with PPI priors.
Criticism for Suppinger. The DE \(p\)-value in Equation 7.2 assumes biological replication (Note 5.2). The permutation null on \(\Delta\mathrm{pc}\) among cells of one gastruloid is again a technical null. INDEED is also ad hoc: it tests edges after two separate glasso fits rather than estimating \(\Delta\) under a joint loss. Use it, if at all, as a ranking heuristic on \(\mathcal{G}_{0}\), with \(p_{g}^{\mathrm{DE}}\) replaced by a fold-change or \(F\) score.

title: 3  Feature selection for cell-type Gaussians
text:
7.2 D-trace: a loss that targets \(\Delta=\Theta_{j}-\Theta_{\ell}\)
Zhang and Zou (Zhang and Zou 2014) introduced the lasso-penalised D-trace loss for a single sparse precision, with an alternating-direction algorithm and sparse-recovery guarantees under an irrepresentability condition that can hold when the analogous condition for lasso-penalised Gaussian likelihood fails. In the same paper they note that the graphical lasso estimator of a sparse precision is usually still consistent for the support of the true direct interactions even when the data are not multivariate Gaussian. That is useful background for our glasso / SILGGM branch: off-Gaussian UMI tables need not destroy edge recovery, even though they do destroy the interpretation of \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}_{j}\) as a Gaussian generative precision.
The differential-network extension (Yuan et al. 2017) estimates a sparse difference \(\Delta_{j\ell}=\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}-\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\ell}\). Empirically, D-trace is competitive for differential-network recovery when the difference is sparser than either graph, although hubs and dense networks remain difficult (Plaksienko et al. 2025).
For DeCovarT this is the cleaner perspective than INDEED:

the estimand \(\Delta_{j\ell}\) is exactly “which partial correlations rewire”;
it does not require a calibrated DE \(p\)-value;
it still does not produce a pair of SPD \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\ell}\) suitable as generative covariances.

A workable composition — labelled as a proposal, not as a result — is: use D-trace (or debiased fused graphical lasso) to nominate rewiring genes; retain those genes in \(\mathcal{G}\); then estimate each \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\) on \(\mathcal{G}\) with a method from Chapter 8 that returns an SPD precision.

title: 3  Feature selection for cell-type Gaussians
text:
7.3 Markov boundaries as panel expansion
Once a GGM exists, a small set of seeds (markers, HVG hubs, INDEED / D-trace hits) can be grown by undirected neighbours \(\{g':\theta_{gg'}\neq 0\}\). In a Gaussian Markov random field those neighbours are the Markov boundary: they carry residual information about \(g\) given the rest of the genes. This is undirected conditioning, not DAG \(d\)-separation. Directed path-blocking rules are the wrong language for glasso supports.

title: 4  Undirected GGMs from single-cell transcriptomics
text:
5 Scope of the core pipeline
DeCovarT needs one sparse Gaussian graphical model per cell type at the population (pseudo-bulk) level, not a per-cell precision and not a directed regulatory DAG. The estimand, aligned with the article, is
\[
\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}
\equiv
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{-1}
\ \text{sparse},
\tag{4.1}\]
with undirected edges encoding conditional dependence (Friedman et al. 2008; Mazumder and Hastie 2011). Single-cell UMI profiles are the only observations. They are not the objects that enter the deconvolution likelihood: we use them to estimate \((\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j})\) for labelled types in the Suppinger murine gastruloid resource (Suppinger et al. 2023). Downstream, those parameters discriminate types via mean shifts and precision rewiring, then enter the convolution
\[
\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}
\mid
(\boldsymbol{\zeta},\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}\!\bigl(
\boldsymbol{\mu}\,\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},\,
\textstyle\sum_{j}p_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
\bigr).
\tag{4.2}\]
Some DeCovarT vignettes write \(\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}\) for the same precision; we keep \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\) as in the article Methods.
In scope: undirected GGMs; single-cell transcriptomics only; stationarity (no RNA velocity, no time-varying graphs); labelled cell types (Suppinger annotations), not unsupervised clustering of the graph.
Out of scope for the core, relocated to Chapter 10: multi-omics (ATAC, ChIP, spatial); causal DAGs; temporal dynamics; fused / joint graphs across types; copula constructions such as JGCGM that go beyond a Gaussian or Poisson-lognormal observation model.
Dataset constraint. GSE229513 is a 10x Chromium 3′ v3 UMI resource with one technical scRNA-seq experiment, not independent biological replicates for GRNs. GSE250136 is a later stem-embryo dataset; it is external validation, not extra Suppinger replicates. Technical bootstrap of cells is allowed (Chapter 10); biological bootstrap is not.

title: 4  Undirected GGMs from single-cell transcriptomics
section: 7.1 SILGGM: five inferential modes, one generative precision
text:
7.1 SILGGM: five inferential modes, one generative precision
SILGGM is a frequentist toolkit for high-dimensional GGMs (Zhang et al. 2018a, 2018b). After optional NPN, it takes an \(n\times G\) table and estimates \(\theta_{gg'}\) (or de-sparsified versions) with four inferential procedures, the last of which has two penalty flavours:








Mode
What is computed
Role




B_NW_SL
Bivariate nodewise scaled lasso
Edge-wise \(\hat\theta_{gg'}\), CIs, \(p\)-values


D-S_NW_SL
De-sparsified nodewise scaled lasso
Debiased nodewise edges, CIs


D-S_GL
De-sparsified graphical lasso
Debiased glasso edges, CIs


GFC_SL
GGM estimation with FDR, scaled lasso
Simultaneous tests of all pairs


GFC_L
Same with lasso (tuning for FDR)
Preferred when \(n\) is small



All five share two steps: a lasso-type regularisation (graphical lasso or \(O(G)\) nodewise regressions), then \((G^{2}-G)/2\) asymptotically normal statistics under a sparsity condition on the maximum degree. global=TRUE extends the first three modes to the GFC FDR framework. Outputs include estimators, \(z\)-scores, \(p\)-values, and (for global mode) adjacency matrices at a target FDR.
What the first pipeline got wrong.

D-S_GL is not universally preferred. The SILGGM simulations report that B_NW_SL and D-S_NW_SL can give better confidence-interval behaviour for non-zero partial correlations than D-S_GL. For a small gene set that needs CIs, B_NW_SL is the authors’ own recommendation; D-S_NW_SL is the cheaper alternative at \(G\sim 10^{4}\). For whole-graph FDR, GFC_L is recommended when \(n\) is small (order \(10^{2}\)) because tuning helps FDR; at larger \(n\) the four modes are similar.
The de-sparsified formula is not \(2\hat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}-S\). The Janková–van de Geer estimator is \(\widehat{T}=2\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}-\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}\widehat{R}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}\) with \(\widehat{R}\) the empirical correlation (Jankova and Geer 2015). The first report’s \(2\hat\Theta-S\) is incorrect.
The debiased matrix is deliberately non-sparse. It is built for inference, not as a generative precision. Feeding \(\widehat{T}\) to DeCovarT would export a dense, not necessarily well-conditioned, \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\). The statistically clean composition (proposal) is: use debiasing / FDR to select a support, then re-estimate a positive-definite precision on that support (constrained MLE when the graph is chordal; otherwise a constrained glasso or a small ridge). That separates edge testing from the SPD object in Equation 4.1.

Pros. Fast C++ implementation; \(p\)-values and FDR; scales to thousands of genes; matches the undirected GGM language of DeCovarT; CRAN package.
Cons. Gaussian observations (NPN is a copula patch, not a count model); no dropout / library-size layer; independent cells; independent types (no pooling); debiased estimators are the wrong generative object; on UMI data the authors themselves used \(\log_{2}(\mathrm{UMI}+1)\) then NPN — which is exactly the transform Note 6.1 criticises. That said, Zhang and Zou (Zhang and Zou 2014) report that the graphical lasso estimator of a sparse precision is usually still support-consistent: it recovers the zeros of the true direct (conditional) interactions even when the multivariate Gaussian assumption does not hold. That is reassurance for edge screening, not a licence to treat the glasso point estimate as the DeCovarT generative \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\). We keep SILGGM as a benchmark branch, not as “the” pipeline, and we prefer GFC_L / glasso support plus an SPD refit over exporting D-S_GL point estimates.
It does not model unknown mixtures: subset cells by annotation first. BLGGM (Wu and Luo 2022b, 2022a) is a Bayesian latent-Gaussian mixture with dropout and spike-and-slab graphs. Given known labels it is largely redundant; MCMC cost and a gene cap of a few hundred make it a perspective, not a core competitor.

title: 4  Undirected GGMs from single-cell transcriptomics
text:
7.2 Poisson-lognormal: Chiquet’s PLNmodels versus PLNFGL
Two PLN estimators share Aitchison and Ho’s hierarchical construction and differ in how they estimate \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\).
Observation model (common). For cell \(c\) of type \(j\), library size \(S_{c}\), latent intensities \(\boldsymbol{Z}_{c}\),
\[
Y_{cg}\mid\boldsymbol{Z}_{c}
\sim
\mathrm{Poisson}(S_{c}Z_{cg}),
\qquad
\log\boldsymbol{Z}_{c}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}),
\quad
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{-1}.
\tag{7.1}\]
Zeros are sampling zeros under a Poisson with random log-normal mean; a separate structural-zero (ZINB) layer is not required (Chiquet et al. 2021). That matches Svensson’s critique of automatic zero-inflation for droplet UMI data (Svensson 2020).
Chiquet: variational sparse PLN (PLNnetwork). The PLNmodels framework (Chiquet et al. 2025) treats the PLN as a versatile count GGM and estimates a sparse latent precision by variational inference with an \(\ell_{1}\) penalty on \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\) (Chiquet et al. 2021, 2018). Later work in the same group studies zero-inflation inside the PLN family as an extension, not as the default (Batardière et al. 2025). The exported object is exactly a latent Gaussian precision — the DeCovarT estimand — with a sampling model that respects UMI counts. Fits are typically per condition unless one stacks a group penalty by hand.
Zhai et al. PLNFGL (2026). PLNFGL estimates a moment covariance for the latent Gaussian and plugs it into the fused graphical lasso of Danaher, Wang and Witten: within-type \(\ell_{1}\) sparsity plus a fusion penalty that shrinks \(\theta_{gg'}^{(j)}\) towards \(\theta_{gg'}^{(\ell)}\) across conditions (Zhai et al. 2026; Danaher et al. 2012). That is joint estimation. It belongs in Chapter 10 as a sharing strategy, not in the core independent-type comparison. It is nonetheless the closest published composition to “PLN observations + several related \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\)”.

section: 7.3 Multi-axis GGMs (GmGM): cells are not independent rows
text:
7.3 Multi-axis GGMs (GmGM): cells are not independent rows
Almost every GGM above makes the independence assumption: to learn the gene precision, cells are i.i.d. rows. That is false in a gastruloid — cells share a microenvironment, a lineage, and (in spatial assays) neighbours. GmGM (Andrew et al. 2026) replaces independence with a Cartesian product assumption: gene \(g\) in cell \(c\) may depend on other genes in the same cell, or on the same gene in other cells, but not on arbitrary cell–gene pairs. The precision of \(\mathrm{vec}(X)\) is a Kronecker sum of a gene precision and a cell precision. A Gaussian copula (nonparanormal) weakens Gaussian margins. The 2026 contribution is scalability to millions of cells via a low-rank / linearly sparse eigendecomposition; the Python package is GmGM.
Pros. Direct stress test of the i.i.d.-cell assumption that underwrites both SILGGM and the aggregation algebra in Chapter 8; jointly estimates a cell graph (lineage / communication proxy) and a gene graph; copula margins.
Cons. The statistical object is not Equation 4.1: one gene precision is shared across cells, with residual dependence pushed into the cell axis. DeCovarT wants type-specific \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\), which requires subsetting types or interpreting the cell graph as a substitute for type labels. Kronecker structure is a modelling restriction. Multi-omics shared-axis examples in the paper (RNA+ATAC) are out of our core scope.
Use. External stress test, not the default DeCovarT estimator. If the gene-axis precision on a type subset disagrees violently with per-type SILGGM / PLN, the i.i.d. assumption is a suspect.

title: 4  Undirected GGMs from single-cell transcriptomics
text:
7.4 Sparse plus low-rank latent-variable GGMs
A sparse GGM assumes that, after conditioning on the observed genes, the remaining dependence is sparse. Unmeasured programmes — cell cycle, maturation, sequencing depth not captured by a size factor — induce a dense marginal precision. Chandrasekaran, Parrilo and Willsky separate a sparse conditional interaction matrix among observed genes from a low-rank contribution of latent factors (Chandrasekaran et al. 2012):
\[
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\mathrm{marg}}
=
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\mathrm{sparse}}
-
\boldsymbol{L},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{L}\succeq 0,\
\mathrm{rank}(\boldsymbol{L})\ll G.
\tag{7.2}\]
Pros. Protects the gene graph against global confounders that are rampant in scRNA-seq; the sparse summand is the object one would like to call “regulation”; conceptually close to factor-adjusted GGMs.
Cons. Identifiability needs incoherence between the sparse and low-rank parts; tuning two penalties; the low-rank piece is not a DeCovarT type covariance — it is a nuisance. If the sparse component changes dramatically relative to ordinary glasso, inferred edges may have been global programmes.
Use. Robustness experiment on the same gene panel as SILGGM. If sparse edges are stable, ordinary glasso was not merely fitting cell cycle; if they collapse, do not export the dense glasso to DeCovarT.

title: 4  Undirected GGMs from single-cell transcriptomics
text:
10.1 Fused and joint graphical lasso
Related gastruloid types should share part of their graph and differ on a sparse rewiring set. The joint graphical lasso (Danaher et al. 2012) estimates \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{J}\) together with a group or fused penalty. PLNFGL is the PLN observation layer plus fused glasso (Zhai et al. 2026).
The modelling decision — independent versus partially pooled precisions — is more consequential than glasso versus nodewise lasso. For DeCovarT the risk is shrinkage of \(\Delta_{j\ell}\). If fusion is used, keep \(\lambda_{2}\) small and compare supports to the independent SILGGM / PLN fits. Full joint estimation is not the core default until we can show that rewiring of developmental neighbours is preserved.

title: 4  Undirected GGMs from single-cell transcriptomics
text:
10.2 Gaussian copulas beyond NPN: JGCGM
JGCGM learns several subgroup networks from scRNA-seq with a Gaussian copula and an explicit split between shared and subgroup-specific edges (Wu et al. 2020). The authors warn against naïve NPN on counts. That is the right warning; the method is still a copula GGM, hence undirected and stationary, but it is a joint estimator (appendix) and it does not provide a PLN sampling layer. Use it as a copula-aware fused comparator if an implementation is available; do not replace PLN on UMI counts without a benchmark.
Chiquet’s earlier work on latent organisation, sample heterogeneity, time-course, and multi-attribute GGMs (HDR; SIMoNe; cooperative lasso) supplies structured penalties (Chiquet et al. 2012) that could encode pathway modules. Those penalties are optional regularisers, not a second estimand.

8.1 Independent Gaussian cells
Assume, for a fixed type \(j\) (subscript dropped),
\[
\boldsymbol{x}_{c}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{c},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c})
\quad\text{independent in }c.
\tag{8.1}\]
Affine closure of multivariate Gaussians (linear transformation theorem) gives
\[
\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}
=
\sum_{c} w_{c}\boldsymbol{x}_{c}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}\!\left(
\sum_{c}w_{c}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{c},\;

\right).
\tag{8.2}\]

The first pipeline stated that summing or averaging preserves the zero pattern of \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}\). That is true only in the proportional-covariance case.
If \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) for all \(c\), then \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}}=(\sum_{c}w_{c}^{2})\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) and
\[
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}}
=
\frac{1}{\sum_{c}w_{c}^{2}}\,\boldsymbol{\Theta},
\tag{8.3}\]
so zeros are exactly preserved. If the cells have genuinely different \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}\),
\[
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}}
=
\Bigl(\sum_{c}w_{c}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}\Bigr)^{-1},
\tag{8.4}\]
and inversion does not commute with summation. There is no general reason for the zero pattern of \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}}\) to equal any individual cell’s precision, or the precision of the “typical” cell. Heterogeneous cells within a labelled type — a gastruloid “type” is already a continuum — therefore break naïve sparsity transfer.
What we do in the core. Treat labelled cells of type \(j\) as exchangeable draws from one \(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})\), estimate that law (GGM or PLN), and export it. The affine formulae then describe how a pseudo-bulk of i.i.d. draws from the same law would behave. They are not a licence to average heterogeneous \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c}\) and keep the glasso zeros. If GmGM (Section 7.3) finds a non-trivial cell-axis precision, the i.i.d. hypothesis is already false and Equation 8.3 is an approximation.

text:
8.2 Mean and covariance that DeCovarT actually wants
DeCovarT’s \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}\) is a cross-cell mean of the purified profile, analogous to MuSiC’s cross-sample mean (Wang et al. 2019), not a single latent draw. Empirically,
\[
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}
=
\frac{1}{n_{j}}\sum_{c\in C_{j}}\boldsymbol{x}_{c\cdot j}
\quad\text{(linear scale)},
\tag{8.5}\]
and \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}\) comes from the GGM / PLN fit on the gene panel, not from the unstructured sample covariance of thousands of genes (that matrix is singular for \(G>n_{j}\) and dense). The glasso / PLN precision is inverted (or solved) to an SPD covariance for the likelihood. Scale conventions (\(n_{j}\) versus \(1\)) must be fixed once: the convolution uses \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\) of the population profile, the same object whose mean is \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}\), not the covariance of the cell-average estimator.

title: 5  From single cells to type-level Gaussians
text:
9.1 Discrete OT between count histograms (DecOT)
Kantorovich OT between discrete measures \(\mu,\nu\) with ground cost \(M\) minimises \(\langle M,T\rangle\) over couplings with those marginals. Entropic regularisation \(W_{\gamma}\) makes the problem strongly convex and solvable by Sinkhorn (cours_spatial_omics.qmd; Cuturi 2013).
DecOT (Liu et al. 2022) uses that loss for bulk deconvolution: cell-type reference histograms \(C\) (averaged scRNA-seq) mix as \(CP\approx Y\), and \(P\) is estimated by minimising \(\sum_{m}W_{\gamma}(Y_{m},CP_{\cdot m})_{M}\) with an entropic non-negativity regulariser. The ground cost \(M\) encodes gene–gene geometry (co-expression distances), so the loss is not elementwise \(\ell_{2}\) / KL. An ensemble over donor-specific references follows SCDC.
What survives under our constraints. DecOT is a competitor to DeCovarT’s proportion step, not a way to estimate \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\). Useful ideas to steal:

a ground cost on genes can be the same metric that a GGM already implies (e.g. \(M_{gg'}=1-|\hat\rho_{gg'}|\) on partial correlations) — but then OT and the GGM are no longer independent evidence;
entropic discrete OT is the right language if we align two count histograms (empirical mean cell versus type-level expected counts under PLN);
ensemble over donors does not apply (one resource).

Discrete OT on cells (transporting \(n_{j}\) cells onto \(n_{\ell}\) cells of another type) is a type-matching problem, not population GGM estimation. Semi-discrete OT (continuous source, discrete Laguerre / power cells; cours_spatial_omics.qmd) is the natural model when one side is a fitted Gaussian and the other is a finite cell cloud: the dual weights \(\boldsymbol{\varphi}\) inflate Voronoi cells until masses match. That is a diagnostic of which cells are surprising under \(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})\), not an estimator of \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\).

title: 5  From single cells to type-level Gaussians
text:
10.3 Monte Carlo from generative models
When we need more type-level profiles than \(n_{j}\) cells, or a known skeleton for BEELINE-style AUPRC, we simulate.
scDesign2 (Sun et al. 2021) fits, per cell type, a copula: a count marginal (Poisson, NB, ZIP, or ZINB, chosen per gene) plus a Gaussian copula for dependence. It preserves genes, captures correlations, and can vary cell number and depth. It is transparent (parameters are means, dispersions, copula correlations). For our purpose: fit the copula on the GGM / PLN skeleton (constrain or initialise the copula correlation from \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}\)), draw synthetic cells, re-aggregate, and measure how well \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\) is recovered. Using ZINB marginals should be a sensitivity, not the default, for the same reason as Note 8.1.
scMultiSim (Li et al. 2025) is a mechanistic multi-omics simulator: GRN, chromatin, RNA velocity, spatial location, cell–cell interaction, technical noise. It can take a GRN as input and emit counts — the right tool for a known-skeleton benchmark in the spirit of BEELINE / SERGIO / dyngen. Most of its modalities (ATAC, space, velocity) are out of the core. The transcriptomic channel with a user GRN is in scope for metrics (Chapter 9). Do not fit scMultiSim’s full spatial/CCI stack merely to pad Suppinger.
What we reject as a default generator. Black-box GANs; simulators that do not preserve gene identity; using SERGIO’s random GRN as if it were gastruloid biology. The improved pipeline’s suggestion to feed the sparse GGM into scDesign2 / scMultiSim as a prior is the right benchmark design, not a way to invent biological replicates.

title: 6  Evaluating networks without a true DAG
text:
7 What we are not claiming
There is no complete ground-truth GRN for murine gastruloids. Mouse TF catalogues are incomplete; ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq are not measured in the core Suppinger scRNA-seq table we use for \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\); and undirected GGM edges are not the same objects as directed TF–target arrows. Evaluation must therefore be relative (methods against each other, against perturbed data, and against partial priors), not a claim of causal recovery.
This chapter groups metrics into three families, following GRETA’s split of mechanistic / predictive / literature tasks and BEELINE’s emphasis on precision–recall against synthetic or curated graphs:
Directed causal metrics, multimodal ATAC/ChIP recovery, and perturbation forecasting are perspectives: they judge a different estimand than Equation 4.1.
BEELINE evaluated directed GRN algorithms, often on pseudotime-ordered cells, against synthetic Boolean networks and curated TF–gene graphs. GRETA evaluated multimodal (RNA+ATAC) pipelines on mechanistic perturbation tasks, predictive reconstruction of omics, and literature databases. Our core graphs are undirected, stationary, and transcriptomics-only. We therefore:

title: 6  Evaluating networks without a true DAG
text:
8.1 Resampling and noise
With one experiment, the honest uncertainty is conditional on this atlas:

Technical cell bootstrap within type, labels fixed (Chapter 10). Re-estimate \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\); record edge inclusion frequencies (stability selection in the sense of Meinshausen and Bühlmann (Meinshausen and Bühlmann 2010)) and the Frobenius / Bures spread of \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}\).
Gene or cell downsampling, as GRETA does to test sensitivity to coverage. GRETA found that TF and gene sets can look stable while edges collapse under downsampling — a warning we should expect for glasso supports as well.
Random seeds for stochastic estimators (GmGM, Bayesian graphs, boosting). GRETA reported that some multimodal methods reverse high-weight edges across seeds; a GGM that needs a seed should publish edge-overlap across seeds.
Observation-model contamination (Gaussian, \(t_{\nu}\), PLN, extra zeros) belongs with Chapter 8, not as a graph-recovery score.

Biological (multi-organoid) bootstrap is unavailable. Reporting a bootstrap interval as if it were between-experiment uncertainty would repeat the pseudoreplication error of Note 5.2.

8.3 Distances between type-level Gaussians
Closed forms, for non-degenerate \(P_{j}=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})\):
Kullback–Leibler
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{j}\parallel P_{\ell})
&=
\tfrac12\Bigl[
\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})
+(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot\ell}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j})^{\top}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}^{-1}
(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot\ell}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j})
-G
+\ln\frac{\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}}{\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}}
\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.1}\]
Jeffreys \(J(P_{j},P_{\ell})=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{j}\parallel P_{\ell})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\ell}\parallel P_{j})\) is the symmetric version used as a separation monitor in the feature chapter.
Hellinger via Gaussian affinity, and MixSim overlap \(\omega_{j\ell}=\Omega_{j\ell}+\Omega_{\ell j}\) as the sum of misclassification probabilities (Melnykov et al. 2012, 2021), are the right “can DeCovarT tell these types apart?” scores. They are not graph metrics; they are metrics on the generative object.
Bures–Wasserstein (Chapter 9) splits mean displacement from covariance geometry. Use it both as a type-separation diagnostic and as an alignment loss between single-cell clouds and type-level Gaussians.






Note 8.1: :information_source: Compare laws on the DeCovarT scale



KL between NPN-space Gaussians is not KL between count-scale pseudo-bulks. After each estimator has exported Equation 8.1, compute KL / Hellinger / \(W_{2}\) / MixSim on that Gaussian, the one that enters the convolution. Otherwise a “better” SILGGM graph can win on NPN likelihood and lose as a deconvolution prior.

9.1 Skeleton scores (BEELINE, reduced to undirected)
BEELINE (Pratapa et al. 2020) is the standard scRNA-seq GRN benchmark. Its headline findings that survive our constraints:

methods that do not require pseudotime were generally more accurate — convenient, because we assume stationarity;
recovery is easier on simple synthetic networks than on curated Boolean models.

AUROC is too optimistic on sparse graphs; prefer AUPRC

\(|A-\tilde A|\) on undirected edges
Scale with \(G\); report also normalised SHD

9.3 Visualisations
The aim is to compare structure and inference, not to decorate a methods section. Each display should answer one question.
Supports and concordance

Binary adjacency heatmaps, genes ordered by a common hierarchical clustering (from a consensus distance \(d_{ab}=1-\bar r_{ab}\) of methods, or from a biological ordering). Side-by-side heatmaps of \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}_{j}\) for two types make rewiring visible; a third panel of \(|\hat\theta^{(j)}_{gg'}-\hat\theta^{(\ell)}_{gg'}|\) is the differential-network view.
Upset plots or Jaccard heatmaps of edge sets across the four core methods.
On-diagonal degree bars or a simple graph drawing only for a tiny TF subgraph; whole-transcriptome hairballs are not figures.

Signed partial correlations

Diverging tiles of partial correlations \(-\theta_{gg'}/\sqrt{\theta_{gg}\theta_{g'g'}}\) with a midpoint scale, not viridis (the latter encodes magnitude, not sign). Keep gene order shared across types.

Stability

Edge-inclusion frequencies from the technical bootstrap as a heatmap or as a reliability curve (precision among edges with inclusion \(>t\), as \(t\) varies).
Sankey or alluvial only when nodes have a natural order (time, lineage). For unordered type-to-type edge flow, a chord diagram is the usual display; we do not need one in the core stationary analysis.

Distributional alignment (ties into Chapter 6)

PCA / UMAP of cells with the type-level Gaussian as an ellipse is a cartoon (UMAP is not a Gaussian space). Prefer plots of \(W_{2}\) or KL against bootstrap replicates, or rainclouds of \(\hat p\) from DeCovarT under each GRN method (package helpers plot_mc_raincloud(), plot_mc_forest()), once simulations exist.

GRETA-style genome tracks (TF–CRE–gene) require ATAC and are perspective-only (Chapter 11).

text:
10.1 GRETA’s three buckets, restricted to undirected transcriptomics
GRETA (Badia-i-Mompel et al. 2025) modularises multimodal GRN pipelines and scores them as mechanistic, predictive, and literature-based. Core carry-over:
Literature / knowledge

Marker TFs: is a known type marker present as a hub, or as a high-degree node in \(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}_{j}\) for that type?
TF–target edges: if \(g\) is a TF and \(g'\) a curated target, does the undirected edge \(\{g,g'\}\) appear? This is GRETA’s “known interaction” idea with orientation dropped. Resources: CollecTRI, DoRothEA, and mouse TF catalogues — all incomplete.
TF–TF via shared targets: two TFs that share many neighbours may reflect a complex or an artefact of co-expression; report overlap with PPI / IntAct only as a soft score.
TF-binding / CRE / eQTL recovery: GRETA’s ChIP-Atlas, ReMap, ENCODE, eQTL tasks need sequence assays we do not use in the core.

Predictive (observational)

How well does the graph topology predict held-out expression (gene \(\sim\) neighbours), as in GRETA’s “Omics” scores? For a GGM this is almost circular (the model is a prediction of each node given the rest), but a held-out cell nodewise \(R^{2}\) is still a useful calibration: a graph that does not predict expression of its own nodes is a bad Gaussian.
Gene-set enrichment of modules (Hallmark, KEGG, Reactome) is a sanity check, not a causal test.

Mechanistic (perturbation) — perspective. GRETA found that multimodal GRNs struggle to capture causal relationships from perturbation assays, even when predictive and literature scores look decent. That result should humble any claim that our undirected \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\) is a regulatory mechanism. We do not have a gastruloid TF knockout atlas in the core pipeline; we therefore do not use TF-activity enrichment after perturbation as a gate for DeCovarT.
GRETA’s other operational warnings that apply unchanged: methods are sensitive to random seeds and to replacing a single pipeline step; paired versus unpaired multiome changes edges even when cell-type abundances look similar; de novo GRN inference from observational data is close to ill-posed. Our four-estimator design is a response to that ill-posedness, not a claim that one method is true.

text:
10.2 Integer programmes and Boolean models
CORNETO (Rodriguez-Mier et al. 2025) reformulates knowledge-driven network inference as a joint constrained optimisation problem (LP / MILP) over prior knowledge networks: undirected PPI, signed directed signalling, or metabolic hypergraphs. It is not a GGM. As a perspective scorer, it can take our data-driven support (or a TF–target list derived from it) and ask whether a sparse subnetwork of a PKN explains the omics under flow / Steiner / CARNIVAL constraints. That tests mechanistic plausibility, not Gaussian fit. Joint multi-sample inference is CORNETO’s selling point; with one gastruloid experiment we would be back to a single-sample PKN extract.
Boolean / logical models (the BEELINE curated networks; BoolODE) are simpler mechanistic simulators: truth tables \(\to\) ODEs \(\to\) synthetic counts. They supply a known skeleton for AUPRC when we simulate (Section 10.3). They are not fitted to Suppinger as the DeCovarT graph. Using a Boolean model as the prior and a GGM as the data-driven proposal is a legitimate consistency check; using the Boolean model as \(\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\) would abandon the Gaussian convolution.
